content:
Since Tau Ceti has been up and running for a while now, I was wondering what people thought about the quality of the code being produced in it? In particular:

  1. Does it meet the expectations of those who wrote the roadmaps?
  2. How does it compare to the quality of code in Mathlib?
  3. Are the usual follies of AI generated code being avoided?

(Particularly interested in hearing from experts in the areas which have been formalized into Tau Ceti already).

So I was thinking of trying to do a deep dive once we hit a million lines of code (which should happen today or tomorrow), but overall one thing that seems to be happening is that if you are taking autoformalisation projects from other repos and PRing it to Tau Ceti, then usually the code quality improves quite a bit. It seems like starting from the ground up, but using the existing code as a guide (as well as getting more basic API done early, tagging things with simp and grind, etc) works quite well.

Some observations: with Tau Ceti rubrics, and given the current review mechanism, the quality of PRs converge to meet a basic bar much better than many autoformalizations without such rubrics but still far from mathlib quality. There are also residual issues missed by reviewer agents introduced while addressing requested changes. They are obvious or suspicious to eyeballing but may or may not be fixed by later unconcious refactoring by agents when the initial pass on a roadmap is done. So I have and would keep a low expection of the quality purely by agents but I think that's exactly the baseline which contributors are working towards.

Agents thought less about math and overall coherence, they optimize locally for the PR scope and its deps. There are many ways to prove the same goal and the agent might settle on a mechanical shortcut but not natural for mathematicians. There are many chemical reactions between roadmaps that would have happened during mathlib PRs but not happening here yet. The feedback loop from working on a roadmap to revising that roadmap has not been established yet.

Finishing a roadmap or even a few passes of unconcious refactoring is only the starting point, they need more conscious considerations and refactors, and consumer projects to polish. Those conscious considerations, even if they can be distilled into skills, are more macro level skills or open research skills, and don't seem to be covered by known skills or setup, but worth experimenting with. (In the meanwhile, there are many conscious refactors by Kim already happening in the process.)
